item.title: The Death of Socrates
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: Two decades after The Swing, French painting executed a total reversal — from silk to stone, from flirtation to philosophy. David's Socrates, condemned by Athens for corrupting the young with questions, reaches calmly for the cup of hemlock while still lecturing on the immortality of the soul; his disciples collapse in grief around him. Every line is as disciplined as the moral: frozen gestures, sculptural bodies, a composition as severe as a Roman relief. This is Neoclassicism as ethical program — art to make citizens brave — and viewers in 1787 read it instantly as a rebuke of aristocratic frivolity and a call to principle over life itself. Two years later came the Revolution, and David became its official artist (and a Jacobin who voted to execute the king). At the foot of the bed sits an aged Plato, who was not present at the death and would have been a young man anyway — David knew; the old man dreaming the scene is the painting admitting it is a philosophy, not a report.
item.lookFor: Count the gestures along the frieze of figures: only Socrates points upward — toward the realm of ideas — while every other hand grasps, mourns, or reaches for the earthly cup.
